newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Second-tier data, Fed speech.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Second-tier data, Fed speech.

text.p: Investors hoping U.S. credit markets will soar again Wednesday may find scant support in the day's economic data or a speech by a Federal Reserve bank chief, which experts said may register little impact.
U.S. business inventories for November are due out at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, while Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President Alfred Broaddus speaks late in the day at 1630 EST/2130 GMT.
"I would say neither one probably has the potential to move the market significantly," said Cheryl Katz, a vice president and senior economist at Merrill Lynch and Co.
Treasuries surged on Tuesday after the Labor Department reported a modest 0.1 percent gain in the core rate of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which excludes food and energy.
Although business inventories will provide a further read on fourth-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the report is considered second-tier data compared to CPI.
"There will be something to look at, but again, it's not one of those mainstream type numbers. You can't expect the market to react as much," said Richard Koss, an economist at MFR Inc.

Businesses added to stocks of unsold goods at the fastest rate in nine months during October as total inventories grew by 0.5 percent. Economists polled by Reuters, on average, predicted November inventories increased by 0.3 percent.
Koss said analysts could began to speculate that fourth-quarter GDP grew by more than 4.0 percent if business inventories come in strong and are followed by a robust exports number on Friday.
U.S. international trade data for November are due out Friday.

Broaddus, who is also a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committe (FOMC), will address the Richmond Society of Financial Analysts on Wednesday. The next FOMC policy-setting meeting is set for February 4-5.

"While they claim that everybody has a say at the meeting whether you're voting or not, certainly if you're voting your say is a little bit more relevant to the market, said Evelina Tainer, chief economist at Indosuez Carr Futures.
She added the Broaddus comments will also be interesting because there is nothing else going on.
The 0.1 percent increase in core CPI in December may have cheered credit markets on Tuesday, but it does not guarantee that price pressures will remain fairly tame.
Koss said the market would certainly pay attention if Broaddus raises a flag on wage and price growth down the road.
However, Koss said, "If he (says) things are under control (and) we must remain vigilant, the sort of normal Fed mantra, well then I'm not sure that would be taken so."
Koss noted that Broaddus is not known for making particularly controversial statements but is cable of doing so.
In late trading, the 30-year benchmark Treasury bond stood around one point higher at 96-17/32 to yield 6.77 percent.
Federal funds are expected to open at 5.5 percent on Wednesday.
